title: Rebuild a repository through a stream you can edit
summary: fast-export turns a repository into a plain-text stream of commits and blobs; fast-import turns a stream back into a repository. Between the two you can transform anything — which is how every git migration tool works.
mental_model: The stream is the whole repository serialised: `blob`, `commit`, `reset` and `data` records in order. Anything you can do to a text stream, you can do to a repository — which is why this pair underpins the importers for every other version-control system.
danger: The rebuilt repository has entirely new shas. This is a migration tool, not an edit — everyone re-clones afterwards.

steps.title: Serialise the repository
steps.why: `fast-export --all` writes every commit, blob and ref to stdout as text. Read the first lines and the format is obvious: a record type, a length, then the data.
steps.expect: A text file containing blob and commit records, and three commits.

verify.label: the whole repository serialised to a text stream

steps.title: Read the structure
steps.why: `reset` sets a ref, `commit` starts a commit, `data <n>` introduces a length-prefixed payload, `M 100644 :n path` marks a file. Once you can read this, you can transform it.
steps.expect: The record types that make up the format.

steps.title: Transform the stream in a pipe
steps.why: Here the commit messages are lower-case, an artefact of the original import. A one-line sed on the stream fixes every message at once — no rebase, no interactive todo list, no conflicts.
steps.expect: The rebuilt repository has the same three commits with capitalised messages.

verify.label: every commit message was rewritten by editing the stream

steps.title: Confirm the trees are identical
steps.why: A migration must change metadata and nothing else. Compare the tree of each side's tip: same tree sha means every file is byte-for-byte identical, whatever happened to the commits.
commands: sh -c 'test "$(git rev-parse main^{tree})" = "$(cd ../rebuilt && git rev-parse main^{tree})" && echo "trees identical"'
sh -c 'echo original commit: $(git rev-parse main); echo rebuilt commit:  $(cd ../rebuilt && git rev-parse main)'
steps.expect: Identical trees, different commit shas — exactly what a metadata rewrite should produce.

verify.cmd: sh -c 'test "$(git rev-parse main^{tree})" = "$(cd ../rebuilt && git rev-parse main^{tree})" && echo same'
verify.label: the file content survived the round trip untouched

steps.title: Filter paths out during the import
steps.why: `--no-data` exports commits without file contents, which is how you inspect structure cheaply. For real filtering, `fast-export` plus a stream editor is what `filter-repo` automates — and knowing the mechanism means you are never stuck without the tool.
steps.expect: File marks with no blob payloads — the shape of history without its content.

steps.title: Export a subset by revision range
steps.why: fast-export takes the same revision arguments as log. Exporting only part of history, then importing it into a fresh repository, is a truncation that needs no synthetic root commit.
steps.expect: A repository containing only the last commit's work, with a fresh root.

verify.label: a revision range exported into a new repository

steps.title: Know when to reach for it
steps.why: For removing a file, `filter-repo` is faster and safer. For anything it cannot express — renaming authors from a lookup table, merging two histories, importing from another system — the stream is the escape hatch, and it is always available.
commands: sh -c 'cd ../rebuilt && git fsck --full --no-dangling && echo "rebuilt repository is healthy"'

verify.label: the rebuilt repository is structurally sound
every commit message was rewritten through the stream

verify.cmd: sh -c 'test "$(git rev-parse main^{tree})" = "$(cd ../rebuilt && git rev-parse main^{tree})" && echo same'
verify.label: …while every file stayed byte-for-byte identical
a partial export rebuilt a smaller repository
the original repository was never modified — export only reads

pitfalls: Every commit in the rebuilt repository has a new sha. Treat it as a migration: announce it, and have everyone re-clone.
`fast-import` writes into whatever repository it is run in. Always import into a fresh `git init`, never into a working repository.
Signatures do not survive the round trip — a signed tag comes out unsigned unless you re-sign it.
For common tasks (`--path`, `--invert-paths`, mailmap rewrites) `git filter-repo` is faster, safer and better tested. Reach for the raw stream only when it cannot express what you need.
Use `--export-marks` and `--import-marks` for incremental conversions; without them a second run re-imports everything and duplicates the history.
